summary: Johann II Bernoulli studied at the University of Basel from around 1724 to 1729. He later held a post at the University of Basel from approximately 1743 to 1790 and taught Johann III Bernoulli.

Active in Indology and history/archaeology, Johann III Bernoulli earned a doctorate in philosophy from Basel under Johann II Bernoulli and Daniel Bernoulli, also attending Neuchâtel. He served as Royal Astronomer and director at Berlin Observatory and Director at the Prussian Academy.
Johann Jakob Engel was a philosopher who studied at the University of Rostock (~1757–1762) and the University of Leipzig (~1762–1765). He later taught Wilhelm von Humboldt.

An Indologist, Johann Jakob Meyer studied at Concordia Senior College and Concordia Seminary before completing his Ph.D. under Carl Darling Buck at the University of Chicago (1898–1900). He served as a docent at the University of Chicago from 1908 to 1919.

Johann Kirste worked in Indology and linguistics, studying at Graz, Jena, Leipzig, Berlin, Vienna (Ph.D.), and Paris under scholars including Georg Bühler. He held posts at the University of Vienna and the University of Graz, becoming ordinary professor in 1902.

Johann Peter Rottler, a scholar of Indology and linguistics, studied at the University of Strasbourg. He served at the Danish-Halle Mission, superintendent of Tranquebar Botanical Garden, secretary and chaplain at Female Orphan Asylum, and at Vepery Mission.

Johann Philipp Fabricius worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied law at the University of Giessen (~1728–1732) and theology at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1732–1739), later succeeding Benjamin Schultze in 1742.

Johann Reinhold Forster studied at Joachimsthalsches Gymnasium (~1745–1748) and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (1753–1765). In 1780, he was appointed Professor of Natural History at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg.

Johann Tobias Beck was a religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Tübingen from 1822 to 1826. He held posts at the University of Basel (~1836–1843) and the University of Tübingen (~1843–1878).

Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff, active in Indology, studied at the University of Tübingen (~1791–1795). He later held academic posts at the University of Tartu (~1803–1809), University of Würzburg (~1809–1818), and University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1818–1835).

An Indologist and archaeologist, she earned degrees at Leiden and Utrecht (Ph.D. under Jan Gonda). She taught at Utrecht, Groningen, and Cambridge, and served as Director of the Institute of South Asian Archaeology at the University of Amsterdam (1958–1983).

Johanna Narten worked in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology. She studied at Saarland University and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg under Karl Hoffmann, where she later served as an assistant (1973–1977).

Johannes Baunack was a scholar of linguistics and Indology who completed his Ph.D. at the University of Leipzig under Georg Curtius, Friedrich Zarncke, and Hermann Brockhaus. He later served as a teacher and Oberlehrer at Alte Nikolaischule.

Johannes Beltz works in Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Halle-Wittenberg, Lausanne, and EPHE under Marie-Louise Reiniche and Johannes Bronkhorst. His posts include Heidelberg University (1996–2001) and the Museum Rietberg (2001).

Indologist, philosopher, and Buddhist studies scholar Johannes Bronkhorst studied at VU Amsterdam, Rajasthan, Pune (Ph.D. under S.D. Joshi), and Leiden. He worked at Leiden and the Kern Institute, and was professor at the University of Lausanne (1987–2011/2025).
Johannes Brune was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Kiel University from 1903 to 1909, earning a Ph.D. During his studies, he was taught by Paul Deussen and Hermann Oldenberg.

Specializing in religious studies and Iranian/Central Asian studies, Lehmann studied at Copenhagen and Leiden under Fausbøll and Tiele. He held posts at Copenhagen, became Professor of Theology at Berlin (1910–1913), and Professor of Religion at Lund (1913–1928).

Johannes Friedrich was a scholar of linguistics and history/archaeology. He studied at the University of Leipzig (~1911–1919) and held academic posts at Leipzig (~1924–1950) and the Free University of Berlin (~1950–1961).

An Indologist and historian/archaeologist, Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis studied at Leiden University (~1934–1939). He later held posts at SOAS University of London (~1957–1981) and as Professor at Leiden University (1978–1986).
Johannes Haeberlin was an Indologist. He studied at the Basel Mission Seminary in 1827 and at the Church Missionary Society College in Islington in 1830.
